It would be tough to stomach the amount of Tums we would need to ride that roller coaster. My Guy Sleeper Breakout Value Rookie Bust Injury Concerns Colety Crusaders Redraft Rankings 9/2/2026

We are a pro-Sinnott pod here, and we are holding on to a wing and a prayer. We loved the draft capital of the second round in 2024, but since joining the league, he has 18 total targets. But, hey… he caught 16 of them! The departure of Zach Ertz piqued our interest again, only to have it smushed like a bug with the signing of Chig Okonkwo. The ultra-athletic Sinnott should sadly not be anywhere near your redraft radar.

In his third year in the league, Strange was given the keys to the Jacksonville TE room with the departure of Evan Engram. There was a clear connection with Trevor Lawrence, as Strange had a 77% catch rate, including five weeks as TE10 or better. Unfortunately, he was out for five weeks due to injury, and now the team double-dipped in the TE well with rookies Nate Boerkircher and Tanner Koziol. We are fairly high on the Jags offense and the value of Trevor Lawrence this year, making Strange a potential cheap late-round pick. If you have a deeper bench, Strange might be worth a shot to see how the team looks out of the gate.

Who has two thumbs and might be the only legitimate pass-catching option on his team in 2026? This guy! Bowers followed up his incredible TE1 rookie season in 2024 with a TE8 finish in 2025, which, honestly, feels almost just as successful given the state of the QB and organization in Vegas. His targets per game dropped from 9.0 to 7.1, but he broke through with seven TDs in only 12 games played. Add in some competent QB play, either in the form of Kirk Cousins or Fernando Mendoza, and Bowers could rival Trey McBride’s 169 targets of last year. There is so little target competition in Las Vegas that he could break fantasy in 2026.

All hail the ultimate cardio king! Otton ran the fourth most routes among TEs in 2025 (540!) and was on the field for the third most passing plays (625!). Obviously, he crushed it in fantasy football, right? RIGHT? Exactly. Otton finished the season with only one TD, reminding us that fantasy football and real-life football regularly do not align. On a team full of offensive weapons, including two solid pass-catching RBs, Otton’s time in the sun is almost set. But hey, if your league gets fantasy points for getting your steps in, Otton should be the first off the board.

The former Ravens TE signed a 3-year free agent deal with $17 million guaranteed to be part of Mike McDaniels' revamped Chargers offense. We expect more heavy personnel this year in Los Angeles with multiple TEs and a fullback on the field making Kolar a sneaky name to monitor. His college receiving profile at Iowa State was legit but it is more likely that he hurts Oronde Gadsden II's fantasy value more than become an asset himself.

Chig had his moments in Tennessee, flashing some YAC-ability but never quite being a consistent fantasy threat. He signed a three-year contract with the Washington Commanders, breathing new life into his fantasy prospects on a roster that desperately needs another pass-catcher opposite WR Terry McLaurin. You won’t have to pay too much to take a shot on the guy, so why not? He looks like an easy stash or waiver wire pickup early in the season. Chig is not dead for fantasy yet, we say!

After five seasons of “who’s that guy” in Los Angeles, 2025 turned into “hey, I know that guy” for Colby Parkinson. He set career highs in targets (56), yards (408), and TDs (8!!). The TDs are certainly an outlier, but he was a certifiable red zone weapon, seeing 22 red zone targets inside the 20, just three shy of Puka Nacua. We are paying attention, Mr. Parkinson. The only problem is Sean McVay loves TEs, and with a crowded room, you won’t know what weeks to start Parkinson or any of the other Rams TEs.

The offensive weapons in Chicago are plenty, and Kmet tried desperately to contribute in 2025. Unfortunately, the 347 receiving yards on 48 targets - although helpful for the NFL team - were not helpful for our fantasy squads. We all know that Colston Loveland is the present and future for this franchise, so any hope of using Kmet in redraft is out the window, barring an injury. And don’t you dare put that into the universe!

Oh, Mr. Loveland. Slow clap for the managers that pounced on Loveland quickly when they saw the promise of a breakout. His Week 17 performance against San Francisco was one that fantasy championships were made of. We were nervous with the myriad of weapons in Chicago and how Ben Johnson’s offense would come together, but Loveland was the clear first read in the offense into the NFL playoffs. DJ Moore has left town, and Johnson proved that what he did in Detroit was not a fluke, so ranking Loveland in the top four seems 100% valid. We cannot wait to see the jump Loveland can make this season.

The TE3(!) in 2025 returns to Philly with the talented rookie Eli Stowers breathing down his neck. After a league-leading 11 TDs last season - the same as Trey McBride, on half as many receiving yards (591) - we can expect some TD regression. It will be tough to start him every week in redraft, especially with all of the offensive options in Philly.

After his rookie season finish of TE11 in 2023, it has been downhill ever since for the guy we were hoping to become Josh Allen’s No. 1 target. His 49 targets only translated to 571 yards, five TDs, and a TE15 finish. With Joe Brady stepping in as HC, the offense should look similar, but there is no guarantee. The team added DJ Moore in the offseason to finally give Allen a WR1, and TE Dawson Knox continues to be another solid receiving option; remember, everybody eats in Buffalo. You won’t feel confident heading into this season with Kincaid as the only TE on your roster as four targets per game will not get it done in the TE fantasy streets.

“Dr. Schultz” definitely took some sabbatical weeks in 2025 - clocking eight weeks where he finished as the TE20 or worse. Ick. But then he also had some weeks where he was the dude, slicing and dicing in the operating room, finishing as the TE11 or better seven times. It was tough to anticipate what version of Schultz we were going to get in 2025, making starting him every week a scary decision. A lot will ride on whether Stroud can return to that magical rookie season production. He has had at least 85 targets in the past six seasons, but TDs have never seemed to be his thing. Schultz is a low-ceiling, later-round option in redraft this season.

Big Darnell (6’7”) continues to be one of the best run blocking TEs in football, but he has very little to offer when it comes to fantasy production in redraft. You are not even looking his way without an injury to the Muth, but even then, would it be anything but cursory? It is cool to just say no, thank you, and slowly walk away.

The Wallerus is back - GOO GOO GAJOO! He had his moments at times last year with the Dolphins, but he was never a full time player and missed time yet again with another injury. Entering his age 34 season, we're not particularly jazzed about a declining player on what should be a low-volume pass offense, but he reminded us last year that he can still be a red zone weapon in the right matchup. Perhaps he'll fine his way into a waiver wire show at some point this season, but for now, you don't need to be drafting him in redraft formats.

Njoku is joining the Chargers on a one-year deal, and he joins a room with the new hotness, Oronde Gadsden, and blocking TE Charlie Kolar. Njoku was quickly usurped by rookie Harold Fannin Jr. in Cleveland last season, so it is unclear how he will be used in Mike McDaniel’s offense. You need to keep an eye on how the team functions and read the tea leaves in case you need to grab him from waivers early in the season.

It is super cool being tied to Josh Allen and a high-flying offense, but neither is enough to push Knox into the draftable range in redraft. It has been a good long while since his TE8 season of 2021. Never forget.

With only a 7.7% target share and 15 catches on 26 targets, Arroyo is clearly the TE2 behind AJ Barner on the Super Bowl-winning squad. The team had the third fewest pass attempts in the NFL in 2025, so you aren’t investing in the TE2 in redraft this year.

The consensus TE2 behind Sadiq heading into the NFL Draft is now connected to one of the NFC perennial powers. After a final year at Vandy, where he won the 2025 John Mackey award as college football’s top TE, Stowers' production profile was quite strong, leading the class in targets per route run. Stowers will be listed as a TE, but he is essentially a big hybrid WR/TE who actually began college as a QB. He will be behind Dallas Goedert on the depth chart, making him hard to roster in redraft in 2026 outside of an injury.

When Engram went to Denver in 2025, fantasy managers were hopeful that Sean Payton might have found his new Joker, but the role never really panned out. Engram set a career low in 2025 with 28.8 yards per game and finished the season with only one receiving TD, leaving us wondering if the TE6 and TE2 finishes of a few years prior were the outliers. Do not get your hopes up too much – the team traded for Jaylen Waddle in the offseason, added rookie Justin Joly in the draft, and, the most important part of the puzzle, they still have Adam Trautman. Targets will be even tougher to command, and you will never know when to start him - just remember the good times.

Oh, George. Times are tough. It is hard to get behind an almost 33-year-old TE heading into his 10th NFL season who is coming off an Achilles injury. If anyone can do it, you know it is Kittle; he has given us six seasons where he has finished as the TE5 or higher! The physical freak who has publicly said he is targeting an early-season return could be a value in fantasy drafts, if he drops far enough. Pair him with a vanilla-reliable TE that you can use confidently in the first half of your season, knowing you can pop Kittle on your IR. If he comes back even close to his past form late in the season, you have some options in your playoff push. We don’t suggest even entertaining the option unless you have multiple IR spots.

You may have forgotten about the curly-locked, marvelous-mustached Greg D, especially since he has done close to nothing fantasy-wise during his four years so far in the NFL. The best we saw from him was a TE30 finish in his rookie season in Denver. However, Greg showed glimmers of promise at the end of last season finishing second in yards per route run among TEs from Week 9 onward. Miami desperately needs pass-catchers considering a WR core of Malik Washington, Jalen Tolbert, and Tutu Atwell in South Florida. No offense to those guys, but it puts Dulcich in a great position to potentially be the target leader for new QB Malik Willis. Greg D also finished second among all TEs in YAC/ catch, only behind Tucker Kraft. He is a name to monitor throughout camp as he potentially could be an early season waiver pickup.

There was mixed chatter around Helm as he started his NFL career with the downtrodden Titans. He was the team's TE2 behind our pinup boy Chig (learning from the best, amirite?), and he put together a sneaky decent season. He had three TE11 finishes or better, and this was with a QB who was sacked 55 (!) times and had the third-worst 59% completion rate. Helm’s usage increased after his Week 10 bye, going from 8.7% target share to 13.1%. With Chig Okonkwo heading to the Commanders, the opportunity is there, making him an interesting prospect to keep an eye on, especially in deeper leagues.

We were uncertain about how it would all play out in the TE room with David Njoku still the de facto TE1, but Fannin came out of the gate hard in 2025. He was the bright spot in Cleveland last season, leading the team in targets (107), receptions (72), receiving yards (731), and receiving TDs (six) all as a rookie with a carousel of QBs throwing him the ball. The offense in Cleveland was abhorrent, but Fannin still managed to join Sam LaPorta as one of two rookie TEs since 2000 with 70/700/6. He now has to compete with rookies KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston for targets, but the offense on the whole looks to have much more potential with Todd Monken driving the bus. He finished as the TE5 in 2025, and he should go around that in redraft, especially with the departure of Njoku.

Henry was quietly the TE6 on a team where he was second in targets with 87, just behind Stefon Diggs with 102. The problem with Henry was that you never seemed to know when to start him, as he surpassed eight fantasy points per game in less than half of his games (47%). Henry’s weekly uncertainty might not improve much with the addition of AJ Brown and Romeo Doubs. Henry seems to consistently be undervalued in drafts, making him an easy trigger to pull at the end or a pickup off waivers as your second TE on a deep roster.

Remember Week 1 of the 2024 season when Likely had over 100 yards receiving and a TD, and the entire fantasy community went, wait whaaaat? Mhmm. The man is now out of Mark Andrews’ shadow and ready to live large in New York. Target-wise, the big competition is Malik Nabers, and behind him are the likes of Darius Slayton, Darnell Mooney, and fellow TE Theo Johnson. We are following the money ($26 million guaranteed) and his connection with John Harbaugh in assuming that Likely will be a significant part of this offense. You don’t have to go after him early to invest in this late-round flier.

The offensive weapons for Dallas were a delight for fantasy managers last season, simply because the defense was nonexistent. Fergalicious took advantage, especially in Weeks 3 through 6 when CeeDee Lamb was out finishing as the TE4, TE5, TE2, and TE10 during those weeks. He set career highs in receptions (82) and TDs (8), but the contributions fell off in the second half. The trained eye will say Ferguson will be due for some TD regression. However, you can trust in the fact that the Dallas D won’t be fixed overnight, making Fergy-Ferg a late-round target who should still get a fair amount of dump-offs in this offense.

For a few weeks in 2025, “Tonges McBasketball” was the hero we didn’t know we needed. With George Kittle nursing his hamstring from Week 2 through Week 6, Tonges stepped up valiantly, giving us at least a couple start-worthy weeks. He had three weeks on the season as the TE9 or better. With Kittle battling back from his Achilles injury, there is a strong chance he won’t be ready to start the year or resemble the same old Kittle when he does. Tonges is practically free in drafts and will be the assumed TE1 on a Shanahan-led team. Consider him a low investment if you need to plug the TE position early.

Sanders is recovering from a broken fibula and will be battling with Tommy Tremble for the top option at the TE position in Carolina this season. You don’t really want a TE on a team with a QB who averaged under 200 yards passing a week, do you? Do you?

“JOE-lee, JOE-lee, JOE-lee, JOE-leeeeee”. All the Dolly Parton fans out there are rejoicing in the correct pronunciation of this fifth-round TE. The converted WR has lower draft capital than we would like, but the team did trade up to take him. Joly had the second-most TDs in his draft class, and his skill with contested catches could make him a solid red zone option for Bo Nix. Do not expect production significant enough to make him relevant in redraft for 2026.

There have been whispers in the bushes every year about a potential Juwan Johnson breakout season, and we finally got it in 2025! His TE10 finish was the best of his career on the back of 529 routes run, the fifth most for the position. It was the rapport with QB Tyler Shough that really greased the gears, and they should be ready to come out firing to start the season. The team added offensive weapons with eighth-overall pick Jordyn Tyson, Travis Etienne Jr., and TEs Oscar Delp and Noah Fant, which likely eats into his target volume. Going off draft boards past TE15 territory means you can shoot your shot with the former basketballer if you had a fun ride last year.

Sadiq’s impressive athletic profile (remember when he broke almost every record at the NFL Combine?) catapulted him into the first round, heading to the New York Jets at pick 16. The question marks related to his usage at Oregon remain, as fantasy managers must question if a man who couldn’t top 600 receiving yards during his final year in college will be successful as a Jet with Geno Smith under center? He could end up second or third on the team in targets behind WR Garrett Wilson and RB Breece Hall, while competing with fellow rookie Omar Cooper Jr. Oh, and there is also a feline in Mason Taylor in the room that Sadiq has to overtake on the depth chart. Between you and me, a dawg always wins over a cat. You probably aren’t counting on Sadiq right away in redraft this year, but his time will eventually come.

Ah, yes, the TE2 last season! As you may remember, Pitts had an incredible final third of the season with four weeks inside the top-10, including his 40-point(!) Week 15 blowout game against Tampa Bay. We are not expecting this from Pitts heading into 2026, so make sure to let your league mates reach for him come draft day. Rankings-wise, he is living in that TE6-TE10 range where players can become almost interchangeable. Aside from Bijan Robinson and Drake London, the Falcons do not have much target competition, so a world exists where he could bolster his consistency and build on his 2025 season. The QB situation and a new offensive play-caller bring more risk and uncertainty than we would like.

The Packers double-dipped in the TE in the 2023 NFL Draft, and even though Tucker Kraft has had the breakout season, it was Musgrave whom the team took earlier (second round). Musgrave had a chance to show why he was drafted earlier when Kraft went down with his ACL injury in Week 9, but he did nothing with the opportunity. He averaged just over two targets a game from Week 10 on, only marginally better than the 1.25 a week he was averaging with Kraft on the field. Either way you slice it, not great.
current_alert_summary: Placed on the Packers' PUP list to start the season with a neck injury; expected to play in 2026 but will miss at least the first four games as a result.

udk_analysis: With Isaiah Likely signing with the New York Giants, all of a sudden, Mark Andrews has life again. The TE19 finish of last season was far from extraordinary, especially as he bottomed out over the final month of the season. Expected TD regression came as well, dropping from 11 to five. Woof. The Ravens didn’t add any huge names TE-wise in the draft - apologies, Matthew Hibner and Josh Cuevas - so the runway exists for Andrews to have a bounce-back season, especially if he can keep up with his red zone target share. He was close to 30% last season.

Meow. Would you be shocked to find out that Mason Taylor led the Jets in targets in 2025? Me. Too. The main reason was that Garrett Wilson was shut down early due to injury, and there was truly nothing else in town offensively. The second round selection in 2025 is immediately trounced by the drafting of athletic freak TE Kenyon Sadiq. Find Taylor a patch of sunshine and let him curl up. He does not belong in fantasy.

Before transferring to Ohio State for his final year, Klare was a production monster at Purdue and showcased target-earning ability that could intrigue at the next level. Unfortunately, his first-year prospects are dim as he was selected by the Rams, who collect TEs like it is going out of style. Los Angeles has Colby Parkinson, Tyler Higbee, Terrance Ferguson, and Davis Allen on the roster, making the rookie just another guy in the room. Sean McVay has shown a strong proclivity to running 13-personnel, so we know Klare will be rotated in.

Always the bridesmaid, never the bride. Mayer will be the TE2 as long as Brock Bowers is a Raider. But wait, you say…Mayer must have tons of value when Bowers is out of the lineup, right? RIGHT? He did give you one TE5 week when Bowers was sidelined last year, but during the other week, he was TE41. This former 2nd round NFL draft pick will be valuable in 12-personnel sets to the Raiders but not for fantasy.

Remember those magical “Sticky Gesicki” weeks a few seasons back? Never forget. Gesicki’s great weeks in 2024 primarily made their appearances when Tee Higgins was out of the lineup, and then in 2025, things got even more confusing with QB Joe Burrow missing nine weeks. Gesicki only had a 9.4% target share last season and will always be left battling on that front with talents like Ja’Marr Chase and Higgins on the field. If he is on your roster, you are only entertaining starting him if one of those WRs is out, and for a guy who only had two receiving TDs in 2025, you don’t need that nonsense.

Boerkircher (pronounced BOAR-kur-chur) was a surprise second-round selection by the Jaguars. The draft capital is enough to make you pay attention, but when you look back at his performance in college, you are left wanting more - he never topped more than 22 targets in college. Just called him “Boerkircher the Blocker” as that will probably be his main task in Jacksonville.

Noah Fant’s fantasy trajectory has pointed solidly down for years. As a Bengal in 2025, he finished with only 34 receptions and 288 yards in a full rotation. He signed a two-year deal with New Orleans in the off-season, landing behind incumbent starter Juwan Johnson. The team also drafted third-rounder Oscar Delp, making Fant no more than a backup.

As much as we like to admit that Travis Kelce will never retire, the man is cake tasting and choosing floral arrangements. The end is near, but is Gray the next man up? Mahomes has never trusted Gray enough to give him more than one season of 49 targets. He will pop up for a TD here and there, but even in the deepest of TE premium leagues, he is not roster-worthy.

Fifth-round draft pick Gadsden broke all the Chargers' rookie TE records last year as he finished with 49 receptions on 69 targets, 664 yards receiving, and three TDs. However, keep in mind that 241 of those yards came in two weeks. It was looking like the potential was high for 2026 with the addition of OC Mike McDaniel, but then the team had to go and sign David Njoku. Throw in blocking TE Charlie Kolar and FB Alec Ingold, and Gadsden’s path to fantasy relevance in redraft this year has gotten circuitous at best. Despite the alluring upside, 2026 feels like a tough route for Gadsden to be counted on in fantasy and likely someone overdrafted in your leagues.

There was a lot of chatter around what could have been with Oscar Delp, but looking at his numbers from college, he never really delivered. He never hit 300 receiving yards at Georgia thanks to competition with some guy named Brock Bowers basically running the offense during Delp’s first two seasons. Even with questions on the production profile, the Saints grabbed him in the third round to add youth to their TE room. He will have a tough time making an impact in redraft this year, presumably buried on the TE depth chart behind Juwan Johnson and Noah Fant.

Is the Muth still Luth? Unfortunately, the answer might be no with only 486 yards receiving and four TDs in 2025. The team gets back the one and only Aaron Rodgers, who had 67% of his passing yardage come after the catch, the highest rate in the NFL. With Mike Tomlin and Jonnu Smith out and Mike McCarthy and Michael Pittman Jr. in, it is up in the air how this offense will function. Look, it’s ok to just say no in fantasy.

LaPorta tried real hard to put together a season reminiscent of his astounding rookie year starting out fairly well with four top-6 finishes before being sidelined with a season-ending back injury. His 12.2 yards per reception were a career high, and his 81% catch percentage is delightful. But what happens now? New OC Drew Petzing catapulted an all-time season from Trey McBride in Arizona so we are left wondering if LaPorta will get the TMcB treatment this season. The Lions have one of the easiest schedules in the NFL, making LaPorta’s later round ADP palatable as we still consider his ceiling and TD upside enticing. However, it's worth pointing out that LaPorta is dealing with a hip injury that could threaten his Week 1 availability, so fantasy gamers need to track his status closely as we head into the regular season.

Ferg-Daddy 2.0 is one of many TEs in Sean McVay’s crowded TE room, including the likes of Tyler Higbee, Colby Parkinson, and rookie Max Klare. We had high hopes for him in his rookie season. He didn’t deliver, running the fourth fewest routes among the team’s TEs and gaining only a 5% target share. Ferguson did show off via the deep ball as he was the league leader among TEs in deep targets (20+ yards) with 15. Tyler Higbee and Davante Adams are not getting any younger, so perhaps we see a patented second-year breakout from the Oregon TE.

Johnson was putting together a decent sophomore season in 2025, highlighted by an average of 4.9 targets a game and a budding connection with Jaxson Dart. However, he missed the final two weeks of the season with an unspecified illness, ending the year with a whimper. All was looking promising until John Harbaugh came to New York and brought Isaiah Likely with him. Now Johnson is the TE2, dropping out of the redraft conversation. What a roller coaster.

After three TE4 or better finishes in three out of four years, Hockenson fell and fell hard. He saw 66 mostly forgettable targets in 2025. He was unstartable almost every week until he tapped out for the final two weeks of the season due to a shoulder injury. The Vikings’ offense will look different this season with either Kyler or “Nine” under center, and with Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison still there, it is hard to consider him in redraft this season, at least until you see how the usage pans out.

Quick, name the best TE on the Carolina Panthers roster. Exactly! On paper, Tommy “High-T” Tremble looks to be the TE1, but with 249 yards receiving and two TDs in 2025, you have to look twice: he is a blocking-first TE. With Ja’Tavion Sanders and Mitchell Evans rounding out this ragtag bunch of hooligans, if you are asked at your draft which Carolina TE you should go for this season, shake your head disappointingly and respond, “None, thank you.”

Quietly the TE4 in 2025, Kelce finished as the TE8 or better every year as a starter, reminding us he is a true fantasy football legend. Louder for the people in the back! He had a solid 851 yards receiving (TE4) with 584 routes run (TE2), and you can continue to expect to see him on the field as Patrick Mahomes’ good ole security blanket. We would like to see that TD total go up a bit - Kelce had five last year - but to be fair, no one on the team caught more than that number. He is a solid later-round pick if you wait on the TE position, knowing this is his latest ADP in more than a decade. Respect your elders.

If you were able to behold the TE season to end all TE seasons, you are probably still singing the praises of TMcB. With Jacoby Brissett at the helm, Trey McBride was unlocked, running 696(!) routes while breaking the single-season TE reception record with 126. He took advantage of various injuries among other Cardinals pass catchers to finish the year with 11 receiving TDs, a massive jump from the two he scored the year previous. We know that the TD total stands quite a chance to regress on a Cardinals team projected to win the fewest games in the NFL. Be that as it may, expect another year of massive volume, giving fantasy managers a positional advantage.

Kraft was on his way to a monster season in 2025, boasting two TE1 weeks and averaging close to six targets a game, until he tore his ACL in Week 9 against Carolina. He was Green Bay’s leading receiver with 32 catches for 489 yards and six TDs on 44 targets up until that point. Despite his major injury, you will still have to pay up to draft Kraft, making him a dicey draft decision. The talent is there, and the targets could be even easier to come by, but also factor in that Kraft might not be ready to go by Week 1.

The beginning of the year was an utter delight for Warren as he produced just one fantasy finish outside the top-12 in the first seven weeks, thanks to the resurgence of Daniel Jones. He struggled near the end of the year, along with the rest of the Colts’ offense, but still posted 817 yards receiving and a TE7 finish on the year. The four receiving TDs felt on the lower side, but this could go up with the loss of Michael Pittman Jr. in 2026. Warren was the TE3 when it came to route participation at 83%, and we don’t see that going down any time soon. He is in that second tier of TEs in redraft that can be fantasy difference-makers even with the uncertain recovery timeline of Jones.

AD Mitchell has always had that tantalizing upside, but he is entering Year 3 in the NFL, and it still remains to be seen if he can play as an every-down complete NFL WR. After being sent to New York via trade last year, Mitchell popped up for some big games down the stretch without Garrett Wilson, but in classic AD fashion, he disappeared for weeks at a time. He will now have a full offseason in the system, so perhaps he can put it all together in 2026. Unfortunately, the target competition is now pretty difficult with Wilson healthy, Breece Hall in the backfield, and the Jets double-dipping in the first round of the NFL Draft with Kenyon Sadiq and Omar Cooper Jr. You do not need to be drafting AD in your redraft leagues, but if Wilson misses time again, he could be a plug-and-play option off the waiver wire.

You heard about it for months and it finally happened... A.J. Brown is now a Patriot. As for the player himself, last year probably felt frustrating as Philly’s offense sputtered and he finished with career lows in yards per reception (12.9). Even in a “down” year, Brown still finished as fantasy’s WR10 and an efficient 2+ yards per route run for his 7th consecutive season. He remains one of the league's best in man coverage as an absolute bully in one-on-one situations. Perhaps a change of scenery with Drake Maye could unlock Brown for another WR1 finish in 2026.
current_alert_summary: Traded to New England on June 1, 2026 (for a 2028 1st-round pick and a 2027 5th); is New England's clear No. 1 WR. Also dealt with a minor non-contact hand/thumb tweak in camp not considered a Week 1 threat.

udk_analysis: Get that money, Mr. Pierce! After years of being a part-time role player for the Colts, Pierce showed out in 2025 with his first 1,000-yard season and cashed a huge payday with Indy. That financial commitment from the team suggests they think he can level up as a top target without Michael Pittman, but it is worth noting that he has never been a high-volume pass catcher, even going back to his college days, so it does take some projection on that front. For context, he has never had more than 52 receptions in a single season in either the pros or in college. There is some volatility with a big play threat like Pierce, so we like pairing him with more reliable high target share guys earlier in your draft.
current_alert_summary: Returned to practice after offseason ankle surgery; Colts GM Chris Ballard stated 'the hope' is Pierce plays Week 1 vs Baltimore (Sept 13), which is not yet a certainty per team language.

udk_analysis: St. Brown is the pinnacle of consistency. He has now finished as a top-8 fantasy WR in four straight seasons, and he has banked the WR3 overall finish in three straight years as Jared Goff’s high-volume WR1. There aren’t many WRs we would want over him in redraft leagues this season, making him a rock-solid pick in Round 1 of drafts.

“Yoshi” is just running around out there having a great time as the WR3 behind Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins. He is good enough to stick around the league and keep his role, yet he’s not going to steal targets from Chase and Higgins. So long as both studs are healthy, Andrei should remain on the waiver wire.

Terry McLaurin figures to be option A, B, and C in Washington. Behind him, this depth chart is yucky. Deebo Samuel is gone, and the Commanders did very little to replace him in free agency. Enter Williams, who has a chance to be the #2 option right away as a rookie. One question mark on Williams is how his game will translate to the NFL after he ran almost 80% of his routes from the slot in college. We expect him to start out as the team’s primary slot WR, and hopefully, he can jump into 2WR sets. If not, his ceiling is probably capped for fantasy. Even so, his ADP is so late that we don’t mind taking a shot on him in drafts and stashing him to see how things play out early in the season.

This is the exact type of player Mike McDaniel lies awake at night thinking about how to get the ball in his hands to flip the field. He has elite, home-run-hitting speed, but we would be really surprised if he is a high-volume player at the next level. Ladd is the top guy here, while Oronde Gadsden and Quentin Johnston should see plenty of looks. Meanwhile, the team is reportedly high on last year’s second-round pick, Tre’ Harris. Expect Thompson to have a few spike weeks, but good luck predicting them.

What happened here?! BTJ was amazing as a rookie, and all signs pointed to a huge breakout in Year 2. Unfortunately, Thomas’ second season in the league was plagued by inconsistency, drops, injury, and poor play overall. Ultimately, he ended up being one of fantasy’s biggest busts of 2025. Entering 2026, we are now looking at this Jags’ depth chart completely differently. Travis Hunter’s usage remains unclear, Parker Washington played so well down the stretch that you would think he has earned a role, and the team traded for Jakobi Meyers last year, then immediately signed him to an extension. Something’s gotta give in a crowded WR room. Right now, we are viewing BTJ as a potential bounce-back candidate on one of the better offenses in the league. Because of last year’s headache and the crowded WR room, his ADP is depressed, so if you are looking for a volatile mid-round option who could pay off in a big way, BTJ is worth a swing in the middle rounds.

Does this name sound familiar? It should! Bryce is the younger brother of superstar NFL QB Trey Lance (We’ll never quit you, Trey!). He gets a boost in the ranks just for that, obviously. In all seriousness, he is a fun player who can help the Saints in a unique role. Running in the 4.3s at the Combine, Lance provides a home run threat in Kellen Moore’s offense. In theory, that sounds good, but when Chris Olave and Jordyn Tyson are on the team, there is unlikely to be enough volume for it to matter for fantasy.

The Dolphins entered the NFL Draft with easily the weakest WR depth chart in the league. No offense, Caleb, but this selection in the NFL Draft did very little to change that. Douglas was overdrafted based on consensus big boards and, analytically, was a pretty weak prospect. Still, if you are in a deeper league, you should at least know the name, as the opportunity to see the field as a rookie is there. If you want to have a little giggle, just go look at the Dolphins’ depth chart.

The former Steeler joins the Giants, and it seems like they have a type. Seriously, can you distinguish the skillset of Austin from Darnell Mooney, Darius Slayton, Jalin Hyatt, and incoming Malachi Fields? They might all be different heights, but their main contribution to the NFL is being cast as field-stretching, nine-route guys! These guys will catch a long bomb once every 5-6 weeks, and you will go, “Should I start that guy next week?” No! Don’t do it!
Ridley broke his fibula in Week 11 last year and is still working back. On a Titans offense still trying to find their identity, Ridley likely will not have a large part.

Tennessee surprised a lot of folks in April when they took Carnell Tate fourth overall in the NFL Draft. That type of draft capital suggests he will be on the field right away as an every-down player with the chance to lead the team in production. It can take time for rookie WRs to develop throughout the year, so even if Tate doesn’t get off to a fast start, he is a player who could really provide a boost to your squad late in the year.

We might have mentioned Tillman as a Sleeper last summer thinking he could seize opportunity as Cleveland’s WR2. Welp, nothing to see here! Move along! The team has a completely new regime and restocked the WR position with rookies KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston.
current_alert_summary: Browns released veteran WR Tillman on Aug 27, 2026; he was on the roster bubble, dealt with an undisclosed injury and missed all preseason action, and had fallen behind rookies KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston plus Jerry Jeudy on the depth chart.

udk_analysis: Lamb had a good season in 2025, but it didn’t feel great considering you likely had to take him in the first round last year. He missed a few games because of the high ankle sprain, and he only scored three TDs. In the game we play, that is just not going to get it done. However, he is coming off a career high 14.4 yards per reception and has now finished with 1,000+ yards in five straight seasons. If that TD variance swings back in his direction, CeeDee can absolutely finish as a top-5 WR in 2026.

Dike provided a ton of value for the Titans, especially in the return game. In fact, the guy set the NFL rookie record for the most all-purpose yards in a single season with 2,427 scrimmage yards in 2025. He is electric in the return game, and that is probably where he will shine as Carnell Tate, Wan’Dale Robinson, and Calvin Ridley run the most routes. He is not fantasy relevant right now, but if one of the WRs goes down to injury, we at least know he can play.

Bell was viewed in league circles as a fringe first-round NFL Draft pick before tearing his ACL in 2025. Because of the injury, he fell to the third round and landed in an intriguing spot. Unfortunately, because of the ACL recovery, we are not expecting Bell to be 100% in training camp, which, for a rookie, is not ideal when you are trying to learn the ropes of the NFL. Look for him to be more of a factor late in the season and in 2027.

At 6’4” and 198 pounds, Brazzell has the prototypical perimeter deep threat build. He will likely compete with Xavier Legette for playing time as a rookie and be a part-time contributor, especially late in the year. We're not expecting the rookie to do much early on given that he suffered a knee injury in training camp that could sideline him for all of August. After all, are we really that excited about the third or fourth option in a Bryce Young offense? No offense, Bryce!
current_alert_summary: Underwent season-ending surgery for a torn LCL (left knee); ruled out for all of 2026. Deep-league rookie WR only, minimal impact on a standard 16-team draft board.

udk_analysis: Can we go into Madden and turn off injuries here? Before that nasty ankle fracture-dislocation in 2024, Godwin was putting up some unreal numbers, but ever since that injury, his efficiency has taken a hit, with his yards per reception declining in three straight seasons. Mike Evans’ departure theoretically opens up a world where Godwin can bounce back, so we do not mind adding him in drafts as a WR3/4 for your squad, but the upside we have seen in the past is unlikely to repeat at this stage of his career. He certainly gets a small boost in full PPR leagues.

Olave was buried in ADP a year ago due to concerns about the Saints' QB room and his concussion history. Fantasy drafters who took the plunge on Olave in the middle rounds last season were rewarded in a big way as Olave banked career highs in targets (156), receptions (100), yards (1,163), and TDs (9) en route to a WR6 finish. Shough for the win! After Spencer Rattler was benched, Olave went on a tear, averaging 15.8 points per game with Tyler Shough under center. The target competition will be more difficult with the addition of Jordyn Tyson, but Olave is one of the most talented WRs in the league, and we love Kellen Moore’s up-tempo scheme. We would not be shocked to see Olave post back-to-back WR1 seasons.

A journeyman of sorts, Kirk lands with his fourth team, entering his ninth season in the league. He has given us two usable fantasy seasons before, and TBH, what’s not to say he becomes the WR1 in San Francisco in a matter of weeks due to their injury luck? Just kidding. Or am I…Just be ready to head to your waiver wire if this happens, but otherwise, he shouldn’t be on your redraft radar, especially considering he's beginning the season on IR because of a calf injury.

Watson’s bug-a-boo since he entered the NFL has been injuries. When he is on the field, he is highly efficient and scores plenty of fantasy points. That was on full display last season when he returned to the lineup in Week 8 off a torn ACL and went on to average 2.67 yards per route run and 11.5 fantasy points per game. The Packers’ depth chart is thinned out entering 2026, and Matthew Golden really struggled as a rookie, giving Watson relatively weak target competition for one of the better offenses in the league. There is a shaky floor with a guy like Watson due to durability concerns, but if you are looking for a high upside WR pick in the middle rounds, Watson can be nitro to your squad.

We will always remember the good times, Coop. The former Fantasy MVP has slowly morphed into a role player at this stage of his career, but ya know what? This man just won another Super Bowl, so he is probably doing okay! We will always love you, CoopaKuppaCoffee, but sadly, your days as a fantasy starter are long gone. We view Kupp as a potential injury fill-in should JSN or Rashid Shaheed miss time.

Sutton’s target share is likely to take a hit with Jaylen Waddle now on the team. Shoot, there were even moments last season where Sutton was losing targets to guys like Troy Franklin and Pat Bryant. For context, he only averaged 7.3 targets per game for a 21.3% market share. If that comes down at all because of Waddle, Sutton could become TD dependent in 2026.

Allen led the Cincinnati Bearcats in targets, catches, and receiving yards in 2025, and his 13 receiving TDs were tied for the third-most in the FBS. He had solid production throughout his collegiate career, but obviously, he fell to Day 3 for a reason. We are always interested in Mahomes' pass catchers, but for now, he is more of a name to monitor in camp than a guy you need to pick in your redraft league.
current_alert_summary: Fifth-round rookie WR (176th overall, out of Cincinnati) has drawn significant preseason praise from Chiefs beat writers; sits behind Rashee Rice, Xavier Worthy, and Tyquan Thornton on the depth chart but is viewed as a potential deep Day-3 redraft flier given Kansas City's WR2/3 uncertainty.

udk_analysis: If you would have told us Darius Slayton was still a Giant after all these years, we would have called you a liar. The team seemed to want to move on for years, and then finally paid him only to draft Malachi Fields and sign Darnell Mooney who do the exact same thing he does - stretch the field. If this were a Facebook relationship, we would give it the “It’s complicated” label. Expect Slayton to be on the field early in the year as Malik Nabers is eased in off his ACL surgery. My Guy Sleeper Breakout Value Rookie Bust Injury Concerns Colety Crusaders Redraft Rankings 9/2/2026

Mooney was never more than a WR2/3 you could use in great matchups, and now he heads to New York to be pretty much the same thing for the Giants. If Malik Nabers is not ready to go at the start of the season, there is a world where he could stand a chance, target-wise, battling with Darius Slayton and Calvin Austin. Monitor training camp and Nabers, but do not expect the moon and stars.

Adams is coming off arguably the best season ever for a WR inside-the-five as he became the team’s “goal-line WR”. He saw the most targets (16) inside the 5-yard line since targets became a stat (1992). Nevertheless, the warning signs are there as he totaled just 789 receiving yards and now enters his age-33 season. When we couple that with Matthew Stafford’s outlier TD season, it is hard to be bullish on Adams repeating as a WR1 for fantasy. We view him more as a WR3, as his price tag in drafts is a bit too rich for us.

He's back! After one season in Washington, Deebo returns to the Bay to reunite with Kyle Shanahan, George Kittle, CMC, and Brock Purdy. Ricky Pearsall is battling a recurring knee injury, and veteran Christian Kirk is on the roster bubble (while also dealing with a calf injury), so the signing of Deebo makes perfect sense for a team that is trying to compete for a division title. We expect Mike Evans and rookie De'Zhaun Stribling to work on the outside with Deebo doing his thing over the middle of the field. Now 30 years old, Samuel's best football is probably behind him, but he is still a solid chain mover on a great offense, which could have WR3/FLEX viability in the right matchups.

Good old DeMario “Pop” Douglas never really popped (see what I did there?) and will be at the bottom of a depth chart led by AJ Brown. With 80% of his routes coming in the slot, he is a bit part player on a depth chart that has bypassed him.

Entering the 2026 season, it is possible Boston is playing behind Jerry Jeudy and KC Concepcion to start the season. For now, we view him as a name to monitor throughout the early part of the year rather than a priority redraft target. Perhaps he can come on late in the year to provide some late-season rookie upside.

Vele goes from WR2 on the depth chart to WR3 after the Saints took Jordyn Tyson with the eighth overall pick. He is not on the radar for fantasy in the long term, but there's short term viability in deeper leagues that have multiple FLEX spots with Tyson starting the season on IR because of his hamstring injury.

Smitty has always been a great talent at the WR position, but his fantasy value has been held in check with AJ Brown on the roster. With Brown gone, expect "Slim Reaper" to be one of the hottest names in fantasy. Smith will have a chance to set career highs in targets, receptions, and yards as the Eagles’ new WR1. His ADP will probably skyrocket, but the excitement is warranted for a guy who’s averaged 14.5 PPR points per game without Brown in the lineup going back to 2022.

The former fourth-round pick is two years into his NFL career, accumulating seven total receptions in 21 games played. He shockingly turned four of them into TDs, but with the arrival of rookie Ja’Kobi Lane and Elijah Sarratt, consider him toast.

The Niners shocked everyone by taking De’Zhaun Stribling 33rd overall in the NFL Draft. He was projected by most as a Day 2 guy, but no one saw this coming. It suggests they have a plan for him, and with Ricky Pearsall battling knee issues at the start of camp, he could be more than just a role player in Year 1. San Francisco did bring back Deebo on a one-year deal after Pearsall's latest knee injury, so perhaps it pours some cold water on the Stribling hype. Still, he profiles as a guy who could play on the perimeter across from Evans, and the camp reviews have been excellent. You can throw a dart late in your draft and stash him with minimal risk. We're in!
current_alert_summary: Rookie WR has been a standout performer in 49ers training camp and is positioned for a notable role in the receiver corps following Ricky Pearsall's season-ending knee surgery.

udk_analysis: It is not difficult to get excited about one of Josh Allen’s top weapons. We do see a world where Moore has a nice season in Buffalo if he can command WR1 usage. That said, in 2024, Allen became the first top-5 fantasy QB without a top-36 scoring WR or top-12 TE. In 2025, he did it again. Joe Brady’s offense can function without hyper-targeting a single WR. Moore’s efficiency marks dropped off in 2025 (just 1.33 YPRR), so we are not exactly sure if he is the same guy he was a few years back. Perhaps a change of scenery will serve him well, but there is a wide range of outcomes here.

Pittsburgh traded for Metcalf, then signed him to a huge deal…only to target him 99 times. What? Why? Needless to say, it was a very frustrating 2025 for Metcalf managers last season in that Arthur Smith/Aaron Rodgers offense. On one hand, Mike McCarthy’s offense should be much more throw-heavy in 2026, but on the other hand, Metcalf is now competing with Michael Pittman for targets and still has Aaron Rodgers or an inexperienced youngster as his QB. Could Metcalf rebound and regain WR2 form? It is possible, but we do not see league-winning upside with Metcalf in this offense.

The Eagles traded for Dontayvion Wicks and immediately signed him to a one-year extension as he has some familiarity with new OC Sean Mannion, who comes over from Green Bay. We ultimately expect him to be mixing in with Hollywood Brown on the perimeter, but unless Jalen Hurts all of a sudden becomes a prolific passer, Wicks isn’t likely to be a meaningful fantasy contributor behind Smitty and Makai Lemon.

The Raiders' fourth-round pick from 2025 was one of those “summer flings”. He gained some steam with a few camp highlights and some beat reporters lauding him to be the team’s starting X. Listen, we get it; summer is a time for being young and passionate. The dude caught ten passes on the season, including laying a goose egg in the receptions department in eight of his 15 games. Consider this a hard “No!"

Can we get this man a QB? We know London is one of the most talented WRs in the league, yet it feels like there is still so much untapped potential given what has been going on in Atlanta. Even though Tua and Penix have their warts, we are closing our eyes in drafts and betting on talent with Drake, who has been targeted on 30% of his routes over the last two seasons. In case you missed it, the Falcons are trotting out some combination of the three stooges behind London: Jahan Dotson, Zachariah Branch, and Olamide Zacchaeus. Let’s get this guy 10+ targets a game and see what happens!

Ayomanor was fine as a perimeter WR last year, but clearly the new regime is ready to relegate the former Stanford Cardinal to a role player after signing Wan’Dale in free agency then selecting Carnell Tate inside the top-five of the NFL Draft. For now, he is not on the radar for redraft leagues.

There are talks of Sarratt moving into the ‘Big Slot’ role in Year 1 in Baltimore, which is kind of intriguing in deep formats. Sarratt is a ball winner who was frequently used in the red zone in college, giving him life as a contributor right away as a rookie in Baltimore. That said, we expect Flowers and Bateman to open the season as the top WRs on the depth chart, and the Ravens have never had a high pass rate in the Lamar Jackson era, so the path for fantasy is pretty thin out of the gate. He is not on the radar right now as a redraft target, but know the name for the waiver wire in the event Flowers or Bateman miss time due to injury.

Respectfully, Gronk. What the heck, dude?! Before Gronk called his man Ee-Meek-Ah Eg-Big-Boo, Egbuka was on fire, operating as the WR1 in Tampa en route to a true rookie year breakout. After Gronk’s snafu on live TV, Egbuka fell off the map, averaging just 3.2 catches and 41.1 yards per game from Week 6 on. If you zoom out, however, there are a lot of reasons for that - Egbuka played through a minor hammy injury, Baker got banged up, the O-line was injured, and Emeka’s catchable target rate was terrible. If drafts present an opportunity to buy back in on the former first-round pick, we are ready to pounce, especially with Mike Evans now in San Francisco and Chris Godwin another year older. Early drafters, however, should monitor Egbuka's health ahead of Week 1 after he left joint practices on August 12 with a toe sprain.

All this dude does is earn targets at an elite level. Since 2023, G Willy’s targets per route run rates are 25%, 25%, and 26%. Simply put, he is one of the best in the game at commanding a high target share. Unfortunately, that hasn't always translated into elite fantasy seasons, but we attribute that to lackluster QB play compared to other NFL WR1s. *Geno Smith has entered the chat.* Sadly, it could be the exact same scenario for Wilson in 2026. The talent is there, and the targets will be there, but the offensive environment could hold him back for fantasy once again. Nevertheless, he is a rock-solid WR2 for your team and gets a boost in full PPR formats.

George! Jason’s My Guy came through in a huge way in his first season in Dallas. His stats are a bit juiced for those games without CeeDee Lamb, but the point remains - Pickens is a super talented WR who plays in a scheme we like with a QB in Dak who can support elite fantasy seasons. The only thing to consider for fantasy is that the ADP for him is higher than it was a season ago, so we are not getting any discounts here like we were a year ago when Pickens was available in the middle rounds.

Germie probably needs an injury to one of DK Metcalf or Michael Pittman to be fantasy relevant this year. We are projecting him to play in the slot for Pittsburgh, and while that role could provide plenty of value for the Steelers, we are skeptical that it turns into enough fantasy points to make him a startable asset. The rookie is worth monitoring throughout camp, but for now, he is nothing more than a late-round stash.

HOLLYWOOOOOOD is still fun to say on the podcast, but honestly, do you have any memory of what Brown did in the 2025 season? Apart from a Week 1 surprise when he saw 16 targets with Rashee Rice out, it was mostly forgettable despite leading all Chiefs WRs in receiving yards (587). Your league mates might be surprised to learn he is on the Eagles' roster in 2026. Apart from having a player named HOLLYWOOD on your roster, it will be impossible to ever start this guy.

Credit to TeSlaa. He got his own drop on the show and he scored six TDs despite seeing only 27 targets on the year. I mean, the guy knows how to score! Unfortunately, that TD rate is highly unsustainable, and he won’t see any volume with Amon-Ra, Jamo, and LaPorta all healthy.

The Bech hive was down bad last year after the Raiders took him in the second round of the NFL Draft, and he totaled just 20 receptions on the season. He absolutely whiffed as a rookie with numbers so poor (37% snaps, 1.26 YPRR) you would bury your head in the sand if you ever publicly championed him. The Vegas WR room is begging for someone to step up alongside Brock Bowers, so perhaps he can see a jump in usage and target share in Year 2. We are rooting for Bech to make an impact, but he is nothing more than a late-round lottery ticket in redraft leagues.

Super Bowl champion and Eagles legend, Jahan Dotson, is now in Atlanta after signing a two-year deal in free agency. Behind Drake London, this WR room is full of some #NastyBoys, and Dotson might be the nastiest of them all. THE cardio king, Dotson has averaged an embarrasingly low 0.63 yards per route run over the last two seasons. It’s hard to put into words how bad that is…

Lane saw a bunch of contested catches at USC, which is interesting considering his slender build. Expect him to start the season behind Flowers and Rashod Bateman in a part-time role with the chance to develop over the course of his rookie season. For now, he is not worth looking at in fantasy drafts.

Meyers’ 2025 was a tale of two seasons. In Las Vegas, it was forgettable to say the least. He posted just one week inside the top-36 from Weeks 1-9. However, after the trade to Jacksonville, Meyers averaged about seven targets and 9.6 fantasy points per game. It is worth noting that most of that production came after Travis Hunter went down for the year, so we cannot really copy and paste his production for 2026 if Hunter happens to play more receiver than corner. Even still, the financial commitment from the team suggests Jakobi will have a real role here. He doesn’t scream “upside,” but if you are in a league that starts three WRs, Meyers can fill in as your third option as a higher- floor veteran.

Coker gained some steam throughout the summer last year as a potential sleeper, but he injured his quad late in camp and then missed the first six games of the season. It took a bit for him to get going, but he did end up posting four top-24 weekly finishes in his final seven games. His 2026 fantasy value will ultimately be determined by Bryce Young’s ability to support multiple weapons and whether or not this year’s rookie, Chris Brazzell, or Xavier Legette can push him for playing time. Right now, we have him as the second option in the offense. We do not mind him as a late-round stash, especially in deeper leagues.

McMillan missed the first half of the year because of a serious neck injury, but when he returned, he did have a role on this team. Now with Evans gone, McMillan is entrenched as the WR3 to start the season. For now, he is probably not on the radar in drafts, but he will be a plug-and-play option off the waiver wire should Godwin or Egbuka get injured.

Nailor was a solid WR3 on the Vikings, catching 10 TDs over the last two seasons. He parlayed his limited success into a multi-year deal to be a starting WR in Las Vegas. If opportunity is your thing, Nailor has an opportunity (opposite Brock Bowers) to see a 20% target share because, well, someone has to! We preach chasing talent over opportunity at the WR position, but Nailor’s draft cost suggests he is worth a flier and bench stash to start the season.

Former Cowboys legend, Jalen Tolbert, is now in Miami in what is probably the weirdest WR room we have ever seen. It is a mix of fringe NFL caliber wide outs and rookies. Shoot, Tolbert could be the WR1 or WR5! It’s a complete guessing game as to how these targets are going to be distributed in Miami.

Let us hit you with some hard-hitting analysis. Ja’Marr Chase is good at the game! Even with Joe Burrow missing a huge chunk of the season, the dude still finished as the WR4 with over 15 fantasy points per game. Finishing as the WR1 overall is obviously in play, especially if Burrow can finally stay healthy and have one of those elite TD seasons. He is well worth the pick early in Round 1 of fantasy drafts.
current_alert_summary: Limited in practice in the week of Sept 1, 2026; HC Zac Taylor said he 'feels good about him' for Week 1 vs Tampa Bay (Sept 13).

udk_analysis: You know what is fun? Jamo ripping off chunk gains thanks to some of that elite speed. Dan Campbell knows this. John Morton? Not so much. Before Guns Mahoney took over play calling, Jameson Williams’ role was frustrating for fantasy as he was used as a low-volume, high aDOT boom/bust type of guy. However, after Campbell took over the offense, Jameson Williams was one of fantasy’s most valuable WRs as he was on pace for 1,400 yards after the Week 8 bye. It is important to note that Sam LaPorta was also out for a big chunk of the season. Still, the point remains: Jamo is crucial to the Lions’ offense reaching its full potential, and he should continue to have a high upside role that is worth targeting in fantasy drafts.

Jauan “Jennayings” (IYKYK) signed with the Vikings late in free agency, inking a one-year deal worth up to $13 million. With Jefferson dominating targets and Jordan Addison one of the better WR2s in the league, we are not super excited about Jennings’ fantasy outlook as Kyler’s WR3. He is likely to help the Vikings more than he helps our fantasy rosters. That said, if JJetts or Addison happen to miss time because of injury, we know Jauan is a serviceable fantasy WR who can be a plug-and-play option off the waiver wire.

If you grabbed JSN in the third round last year, you likely won your league as Smith-Njigba was incredible all year long, leading the league in receiving with almost 1,800 yards and 10 scores. His efficiency could regress after he averaged a silly 3.74 yards per route run, but he is still an easy click in the first round of fantasy drafts as one of the few guys in the league who can command a 30+% target share.

Reed is a talented football player, but we are still waiting for him to put it all together for a full season. He has always popped up for big games a couple of times per year, but he has been a part-time player ever since he entered the league, making him an impossible start/sit decision weekly in redraft leagues. With Romeo Doubs in New England and Dontayvion Wicks now in Philly, perhaps that changes in 2026. If Matthew Golden can’t get it going in Year 2, and Tucker Kraft is slow to return to form off his ACL, Reed could be a sneaky late-round WR target.

For the first time in his career, Jaylen Waddle is going to be wearing a different uniform as he is now in Denver after being traded before the NFL Draft. The situation is clearly much better for scoring, playing with Sean Payton and Bo Nix versus Bobby Slowik and Malik Willis. The talent remains with Waddle, so there is upside here, but be mindful that Payton historically loves to use multiple WRs, RBs, and TEs to spread things out. We would love to say Waddle will dominate targets, but the more likely scenario is that Waddle will have to have a highly efficient season to be a difference maker for fantasy.

A fourth-round pick in 2025, Lane saw limited action in a lost season for the Commanders, totaling just 16 receptions. He will be competing with incoming rookie Antonio Williams, veteran Van Jefferson, and the ghost of Treylon Burks for the WR2 job behind Terry McLaurin. Know the name, but you can ignore him to start the season.

Houston double-dipped in the 2025 NFL Draft on Day 2, taking both Iowa State WR prospects. They grabbed Jayden Higgins in Round 2 and Noel in Round 3, and neither guy really stepped up for fantasy on a consistent basis. Noel was stuck behind Christian Kirk for the slot role last year, but with Kirk gone and Jayden Higgins out for the year, he has a chance to win that slot role.

Is Jeudy a capable NFL WR? Sure. Is he frustrating to watch due to the inconsistency? Yep. Is he a fun click in fantasy? Nope! Judge Jeudy had that magical stretch with Jameis Winston in 2024 (#JameisForever), but outside of that small sample, he has largely been irrelevant for fantasy since he arrived in Cleveland. The Browns took multiple rookie WRs in this draft, so his playing time isn’t a guarantee moving forward, especially with a new coaching staff in town.

The Vikings’ offense was a train wreck last season, with that QB play being stinky, hot garbage. Of course, all pass catchers suffered as a result, including Addison, who is coming off his worst season since he entered the NFL back in 2023. The addition of Jauan Jennings does add some uncertainty to Addison’s target share behind Jefferson, but we have seen enough of him in the league to know that he is capable of posting WR2 numbers if things break his way. Ultimately, Addison’s ability to reach his fantasy potential will come down to how well Kyler plays with Kevin O’Connell.

Whittington is a McVay guy through and through. Before the team’s Week 8 bye, he averaged 62% of the snaps, but the production was minimal. We have noticed that anytime Puka Nacua or Davante Adams was off the field, McVay trusts Whittington to immediately step into their every-down role, especially as a blocker. Ignore at your drafts, but do not be surprised if we hear from Whittington at some point in 2026 if the Rams WRs have the injury bug.

With Kellen Moore’s offense projecting to be among the league leaders in pace and play volume and the Saints not really having a reliable third option in the receiver room, we think both Olave and Tyson can eat this year. Of course, we are projecting Olave as the #1 option, especially after Tyson suffered yet another hamstring injury in training camp. He's expected to miss about two months, which means he's going to miss multiple regular season games. He's beginning the season on IR, which makes him a tough click in redraft leagues given the injury risk unless your league uses an IR spot. That said, if he can get healthy, the late-season upside is real if the Saints offense takes a leap in Year 2 of the Kellen Moore era.
current_alert_summary: Rookie first-round WR placed on IR (designation to return) Aug 30, 2026 after an Aug 13 hamstring injury in a joint practice with Jacksonville; reported to miss ~2 months, meaning he will miss the opener plus several games (a Week 9 return is viewed as a likely target).

udk_analysis: The talent with Downs has never really been a question, but he is traditionally been a slot-only player in the NFL…until 2026? That is the million-dollar question for a guy like Downs, who could see a big uptick in playing time and targets with Michael Pitman Jr. now in Pittsburgh. Indy paid Alec Pierce big money in free agency, but behind Pierce and Downs, the WR depth chart is pretty thin, with the most notable addition here being Nick Westbrook-Ikhine. No offense to NWI, but that is not exactly scary competition to get on the field and perhaps set a career high in route participation. Give Josh Downs more routes, and generally speaking, good things are likely to happen for a guy who has been a strong target earner in his career. He is a fun value sleeper for the 2026 season.

JJetts disappointed fantasy managers who grabbed him early in drafts last season, but was it really his fault? I mean, I think we all know who to blame here…“Nine” was one of the worst starting QBs in football, and you may forget, but Carson Wentz (yes, that guy) started five games while Max Brosmer attempted to play football in the NFL. Spoiler: It did not go well. Basically, we are completely ignoring Jefferson’s 2025 season. He is still one of the best in the game, and while Kyler is not a top-five QB, he is certainly an upgrade on whatever the heck the Vikings were doing in 2025. He is one of fantasy’s most obvious bounce-back players for 2026 and is well worth a look in Round 1 of drafts.

Raymond had a bit role with the Lions as an undersized slot receiver who primarily contributed on special teams. Ironically, he is now reunited with Ben Johnson in Chicago, so he should have no issues carving out a nice little role for the Bears. We do not expect that role to be fantasy relevant.

The Patriots obviously felt Boutte was not a guy to build around with a young QB as they added AJ Brown and Romeo Doubs this offseason. He was the odd man out and on the outside looking in given the depth chart in New England. As a result, the trade to Houston makes a lot of sense for both parties. Boutte actually had a few startable weeks in 2025 (four weeks in the top 20), but let’s be honest: you never knew when those weeks were, and you definitely never had underpants strong enough in your closet to make it worthwhile. The Texans lost Jayden Higgins to a torn ACL in camp, and in a corresponding move, they traded for Boutte in late August. He figures to slide in as the WR2 on the depth chart across from Nico right away, especially with Tank Dell starting the season on IR. Consider him a potential matchup-dependent boom-bust FLEX option most weeks.
current_alert_summary: Traded to Houston (for S Jaylen Reed + a 2028 7th-round pick) on Aug 24, 2026, a week after Houston lost WR Jayden Higgins to a torn ACL, giving Boutte real opportunity in Houston's receiver room (33 rec / 551 yds / 6 TD in 2025).

udk_analysis: The Browns took KC with the 24th overall pick in April’s draft as the first skill position pick in the Todd Monken era. Clearly, they have a plan for the young WR, but this could be a frustrating situation to start the year. Jerry Jeudy and Cedric Tillman could still see some snaps, and the QB room is gross. We like him as a potential breakout candidate in the back half of the season when rookies tend to emerge, and with his ADP likely to remain suppressed due to the stink of the Browns, you can take him late in drafts and stash him to see what shakes out in Cleveland.

"Unc" still has it! The 34-year-old signed a one-year deal with the Colts in mid-August to link up with his former OC, Shane Steichen. The vet was quietly productive last year in Los Angeles leading the team with 81 receptions. Obviously, his best days are behind him but the savvy veteran still knows the nuances of getting open in zone coverage in the short area of the field. With Alec Pierce likely starting the year slowly recovering from his injury, old man Keenan could have some WR3/FLEX weeks in full PPR leagues. The key for fantasy is going to be figuring out how this affects his new teammates as he and Josh Downs are both best when playing out of the slot.
current_alert_summary: Arrested early morning Aug 30, 2026 in Indianapolis on preliminary charges of operating a vehicle while intoxicated; released from jail the same day. No NFL suspension announced as of Sept 1-2, 2026; reported to be expected to play Week 1 vs Baltimore.

udk_analysis: Bourne will randomly pop up for monster games as he did in Weeks 5 and 6 last year. He hit 142 receiving yards exactly in back-to-back games and then (get this) averaged 18 receiving yards per game the rest of the year. Impress your buddies at your draft, saying “oh yeah, that guy is a Cardinal” before crossing him off your draft list.

Brad Holmes and Dan Campbell love to draft some dawgs with some grit. Hey, Law at least has that going for him. He is built like a RB and forced plenty of missed tackles in college. Unfortunately, the rookie tore his ACL in early June and will miss all of 2026. My Guy Sleeper Breakout Value Rookie Bust Injury Concerns Colety Crusaders Redraft Rankings 9/2/2026

With the addition of DJ Moore and the drafting of Skyler Bell, he falls further and further down the depth chart. The man can’t separate, and he shouldn’t be considered in redraft this year - even with Josh Allen throwing the ball.

Shakir has been a great target earner in the NFL, seeing 23% and 21% target shares each of the last two seasons. However, his aDOT is nonexistent, and he is not really involved in the red zone. For fantasy, Shakir gets a small bump in full PPR, but you are never winning your league because of him, especially with DJ Moore now in town.

The 3rd round pick was barely involved as a rookie and now with the arrival of A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs, he looks very unlikely to be a fantasy asset in 2026. Sorry Williams truthers but a 4% target share as a rookie is not going to get it done.

We love us some Ladd, but his sophomore season was a relative disappointment, regressing in every major statistical category compared to his WR11 finish as a rookie. He particularly struggled versus zone coverage (1.31 YPRR) as a predominantly slot WR (65% of routes) while ceding meaningful targets to old man Keenan Allen. It remains to be seen if he will be consistently on the field in 2WR sets as new OC Mike McDaniel historically adds a fullback on the field to mess with WR usage. We have Ladd ranked as a solid WR3/FLEX for fantasy and the target leader for the Chargers. However, with a ton of mouths to feed, it will be hard to return to the glory of his rookie season based on receiving efficiency alone.

Last year’s second-round pick didn’t do much early on, but when he got his chance, he capitalized, particularly during Chicago’s playoff run. The Bears are obviously counting on Burden to take a big step forward this season after trading DJ Moore to the Bills, but it takes a lot of projection to buy into Burden’s juiced-up ADP. He is the hotness right now in Chicago’s WR room, but we need to remember he only earned 60 total targets for a 12.8% target share as a rookie. A bet on Burden is a bet on the talent profile and Ben Johnson using him to his full potential. We are viewing him as a high-upside pick who could provide big-time returns if things break right, but there is also a world that exists where he is third on the team in targets behind Rome Odunze and Mr. Loveland. On August 8, Burden suffered a groin injury in practice and missed a few weeks of camp. He's trending in the right direction for Week 1, but given the high recurrence rate of soft tissue injuries, his status is worth monitoring closely all the way up until kickoff.

If your league awards points for aura, Mack Daddy is the 1.01. The shoeless wonder is a weekly must-see for his interesting stadium entrances. He was a solid player for New England on their Super Bowl run a year ago, but with AJ Brown joining the squad, he is not on the radar for fantasy.

After the A.J. Brown trade to New England, rookie Makai Lemon should step into a starting role right away as a rookie across from DeVonta Smith. The 2025 Biletnikoff Award winner in college, Lemon’s production during his final season at USC was excellent, but the one question mark entering the NFL is whether or not he can play on the perimeter, as he was primarily a slot player in college. Philly’s offense should look a lot different this year with a new OC in town. If he is as talented as the production profile suggests and Jalen Hurts can bounce back as a passer, Lemon has a chance to be a meaningful difference maker for fantasy in 2026 and enter WR3 territory. That said, Lemon might get off to a slower start as he's missed valuable time in both mini camp and training camp because of a hamstring injury.

The Giants traded multiple picks to land Notre Dame’s Malachi Fields, so the new staff likely has a role in mind for him. At 6’5” and 218 pounds, he is a true X receiver. Unfortunately, for fantasy, Fields looks like a guy who is more likely to help the Giants than help our fantasy teams, as he is a pretty weak prospect coming out of Notre Dame. We know Malik Nabers is the alpha when healthy, and the team paid big money to Isaiah Likely in free agency. We would be surprised if he is able to generate enough volume to matter for fantasy, but he could have some TD upside in the right matchups thanks to his power forward frame.

You can squint and see it. To be fair, you have to squint really hard. But if you just keep squinting, you can see a world where Benson sees the field. No disrespect to future Hall of Famers Jalen Nailor, Jack Bech, and Tre Tucker, but this WR room is pretty weak. It wouldn’t be shocking to see the Raiders want to get a look at their rookie late in the season. For now, he is just a guy worth monitoring throughout training camp.

When on the field and healthy, there aren’t many better than Malik Nabers. Unfortunately, the talk all offseason about Nabers is going to be injury, specifically his recovery from ACL and meniscus surgery. It is one of fantasy football’s biggest storylines to monitor throughout the summer. We are projecting him to be limited early in the season, so just understand that Nabers will come with risk in redraft leagues, and it is not out of the question that he could start the season on the PUP list. If and when he does get back to 100%, he is likely to provide a big impact to your team, but you might need to wait longer than you would prefer.
current_alert_summary: Recovering from a Sept 2025 torn ACL (plus a spring scar-tissue cleanup procedure). Avoided the PUP list and has practiced in 9 of 10 camp sessions; per ESPN's Jordan Raanan, 'trending toward being ready Week 1' (Sept 13 vs Dallas), barring setback. Nabers himself has stayed noncommittal on a hard t

udk_analysis: Who is the WR1 for the Dolphins? And does it matter? Man, this Miami depth chart is something else. I mean, what a crew. We honestly do not feel confident in playing time or target shares here because this is a brand-new regime with brand-new weapons and a brand-new QB. The Dolphins project to be one of the most run-heavy teams in the league under a defensive-minded head coach and run-first OC Bobby Slowik. For now, Washington looks like he will have a role as the slot WR in this offense, but we have seen enough of him in the NFL to know that a low aDOT, gadgety player isn’t going to be a difference maker for fantasy, especially in an offense that could be the worst in football.

Alright, Marv. Listen up, buddy. It is make-up or break-up time. We have defended you on our show for a couple of seasons, and Mike even wrote a song about the pants store in your honor! Fantasy gamers were hoping for that classic Year 2 breakout a season ago, but it was anything but. Marv had another lackluster season, with this one defined by inconsistency and injuries that limited him to just 12 games. Through two seasons, he is averaging just 9.3 fantasy points per game. As the former fourth-overall pick, that is just not good enough. The QB room remains a giant question mark, and Trey McBride is the alpha here. Unfortunately, we are at a point where Marv has settled into a boom/bust fantasy option, but the good news is we expect his ADP to slide quite a bit this year compared to previous seasons, and this is a brand new scheme. Is the risk already baked into the price?

This guy is so fun to watch when he is making an explosive play, but through three years, he has played just 32% of the snaps. Darn you, Sean Payton! You tricked us thrice into thinking he could actually be something! We know now, he is pretty much just their kick returner.

Golden’s rookie season was obviously not great. He finished with just 29 total catches and failed to haul in a single TD reception until the NFL playoffs. He now finds himself on a scary trajectory entering Year 2. Historically, WRs with poor efficiency in their rookie season who post virtually zero production have flopped more often than not in the NFL. That doesn’t mean it cannot work for Golden; probability is just not on his side. That said, the Packers are absolutely counting on him after they traded Dontayvion Wicks to the Eagles and let Romeo Doubs walk in free agency. Consider Golden a complete wild card entering 2026.

Michael Pittman in Pittsburgh? We did it! Pitty City…but for real. Indy’s possession receiver over the last handful of years, Pittman should operate in a similar role in Pittsburgh and offers a nice compliment to the more explosive DK Metcalf. Given the state of the QB room (an inexperienced younger guy or an aging Aaron Rodgers), we are skeptical of the ceiling here, but Pittman projects as a high-floor WR3/FLEX option for 2026 given his target-earning ability.

Michael Wilson’s 2025 breakout was…nuts. We almost never see nonproductive WRs pop up for huge games the way Wilson did in 2025, but here we are. The man went nuclear without Marvin Harrison Jr. on the field, averaging seven catches and 97 receiving yards per game from Weeks 11-18. For context, that 17-game pace is 187 targets and over 1,600 yards. Fantasy drafters need to be aware that the Jacoby Brissett pass rate of last season is probably going to regress, and with Marv now healthy, we likely will not see the same target share. That said, there is a world that exists where Wilson is more productive than Marv in 2026. Pain.

For the first time in his career, Mike Evans won’t be wearing a Bucs uniform. Weird! He is now in San Francisco as he chases another ring with the Niners. Historically speaking, there is an increased risk with veterans changing teams at this stage of their career.
